claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially has a high-temperature BCC phase.
Phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is governed by competition between composition-dependent thermodynamic driving forces and diffusion-related kinetic barriers.
Strong pairwise interactions involving Al lower the free energy of secondary phases during cooling.
Slow cooling permits more atomic diffusion than rapid quenching.
Under slow cooling, the thermodynamic benefit of forming secondary phases overcomes kinetic barriers and causes transformation.
Rapid quenching suppresses diffusion-driven atomic rearrangements.
Rapid quenching preserves a metastable BCC structure in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
Cooling reduces the configurational-entropy stabilization of the BCC state.
Atomic-scale ordering and local diffusion of Al, Cr, Co, Fe, and Ni alter the free-energy landscape.
Slow-cooled samples will form ordered intermetallic secondary phases.
Slow-cooled samples may form an FCC secondary phase.
Slow cooling will produce compositional segregation.
Rapidly quenched samples will retain substantially more BCC phase than slow-cooled samples.
The proposed baseline is an as-cast alloy rapidly quenched from high temperature that predominantly exhibits BCC structure.
The controlled comparison varies cooling rate while holding composition, prior processing, high-temperature starting state, and atmosphere constant.
The hypothesis is restricted to regimes where cooling rate is the primary kinetic variable and oxidation or additional alloying reactions do not interfere.
Transformation temperature, secondary-phase identity, and secondary-phase fraction may vary with processing details.
Failure of slow-cooled samples to develop a statistically significant secondary-phase fraction relative to quenched controls, despite sufficient diffusion time, would falsify the proposed mechanism.
